summary.text: The target coefficient is converted to mixed derivatives, and iterating \(\partial_y\partial_z\) gives an alternating binomial sum; rewriting the last two factors via \((1+x)^2-(y-z)^2\) evaluates each summand explicitly at \(y=z=0\). The signs cancel, and the remaining sum collapses by \(\sum_{k=0}^n\binom{n}{k}^2=\binom{2n}{n}\), while the derivative factorials provide the other two central-binomial factors.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
F_n(x,y,z)=(1+x+y+z)^{2n}(1+x+y-z)^n(1+x-y+z)^n.
\]
We prove that for every integer \(n\ge 0\),
\[
[x^ny^nz^n]F_n(x,y,z)=\binom{2n}{n}^3.
\]
All calculations may be carried out over \(\mathbb Q\). Since \(F_n\) has integer coefficients and the final answer is an integer, the resulting equality over \(\mathbb Q\) is also the required equality of integer coefficients.

We use \(\partial_y\) and \(\partial_z\) for formal partial differentiation. Recall the elementary coefficient formula
\[
[x^a y^b z^c]\,\partial_y^r P
   =\frac{(b+r)!}{b!}[x^a y^{b+r}z^c]P.
\]
This follows immediately by applying \(\partial_y^r\) to each monomial. In particular,
\[
[x^n y^0z^0] \partial_y^n\partial_z^n P
   =(n!)^2[x^ny^nz^n]P. \tag{1}
\]
The two formal partial derivatives commute, since they commute on every monomial.

We now split \(F_n\) into two factors. Put
\[
p_1=1+x+y+z,\qquad p_2=1+x+y-z,\qquad p_3=1+x-y+z,
\]
and define, for \(m\ge 0\),
\[
G_m=\partial_y^m(p_1^{2n}),\qquad
H_m=\partial_y^m(p_2^np_3^n).
\]
Thus \(F_n=G_0H_0\).

The linear form \(p_1\) has both \(y\)- and \(z\)-derivative equal to \(1\). Consequently
\[
\partial_yG_m=G_{m+1},\qquad \partial_zG_m=G_{m+1}. \tag{2}
\]
For the other factor, observe first that
\[
\partial_z(p_2^np_3^n)=-\partial_y(p_2^np_3^n).
\]
Indeed, using the product rule,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\partial_y(p_2^np_3^n)
 &=n p_2^{n-1}p_3^n-np_2^np_3^{n-1},\\
\partial_z(p_2^np_3^n)
 &=-n p_2^{n-1}p_3^n+np_2^np_3^{n-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Because \(\partial_y\) and \(\partial_z\) commute, differentiating this identity repeatedly with respect to \(y\) gives
\[
\partial_yH_m=H_{m+1},\qquad \partial_zH_m=-H_{m+1}. \tag{3}
\]

Introduce the second-order operator
\[
D=\partial_y\partial_z.
\]
Equations (2), (3), together with the product rule, imply the particularly useful cancellation
\[
D(G_pH_q)=G_{p+2}H_q-G_pH_{q+2}. \tag{4}
\]
For completeness, first differentiate with respect to \(z\):
\[
\partial_z(G_pH_q)=G_{p+1}H_q-G_pH_{q+1}.
\]
Differentiating this with respect to \(y\) produces four terms,
\[
G_{p+2}H_q+G_{p+1}H_{q+1}-G_{p+1}H_{q+1}-G_pH_{q+2},
\]
and the middle two cancel, proving (4).

Iterating (4) yields
\[
D^N(G_aH_b)=
\sum_{k=0}^N(-1)^k\binom Nk
G_{a+2(N-k)}H_{b+2k}. \tag{5}
\]
This can be proved by induction on \(N\). It is immediate when \(N=0\). If it holds for \(N\), apply \(D\) term by term and use (4). Each summand then contributes one term in which the index of \(G\) rises by two and one negative term in which the index of \(H\) rises by two. After shifting the index in the second collection, the coefficient of the summand indexed by \(k\) is
\[
(-1)^k\left(\binom Nk+\binom N{k-1}\right)
=(-1)^k\binom{N+1}{k},
\]
with the two boundary terms corresponding to \(k=0\) and \(k=N+1\). This is exactly (5) with \(N+1\) in place of \(N\).

Taking \(a=b=0\) and \(N=n\), we obtain
\[
D^nF_n=
\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk
G_{2(n-k)}H_{2k}. \tag{6}
\]
We next compute the coefficient of \(x^n y^0z^0\) in each product on the right.

For \(G_m\), repeated differentiation of a power of a linear form gives
\[
G_m=(2n)_{\underline m}\,p_1^{2n-m},
\]
where
\[
(2n)_{\underline m}=(2n)(2n-1)\cdots(2n-m+1)
\]
is the falling factorial. Therefore, after setting \(y=z=0\),
\[
G_{2(n-k)}(x,0,0)
=(2n)_{\underline{2(n-k)}}(1+x)^{2k}. \tag{7}
\]

To evaluate \(H_{2k}\), set
\[
u=1+x,\qquad d=y-z.
\]
Then
\[
p_2=u+d,\qquad p_3=u-d,
\]
so that
\[
p_2^np_3^n=(u^2-d^2)^n.
\]
The binomial theorem gives
\[
(u^2-d^2)^n
 =\sum_{r=0}^n(-1)^r\binom nr u^{2(n-r)}d^{2r}. \tag{8}
\]
Here \(u\) is independent of \(y\), while \(\partial_y d=1\). Apply \(\partial_y^{2k}\) to (8), and then set \(y=z=0\), equivalently \(d=0\). Exactly the term \(r=k\) survives. Indeed, if \(r<k\), differentiating \(d^{2r}\) a total of \(2k\) times gives zero; if \(r>k\), the derivative is a multiple of the positive power \(d^{2r-2k}\), which vanishes at \(d=0\); and for \(r=k\), the derivative of \(d^{2k}\) is \((2k)!\). Thus
\[
H_{2k}(x,0,0)
=(2k)!(-1)^k\binom nk(1+x)^{2(n-k)}. \tag{9}
\]
This calculation applies to every \(0\le k\le n\), including the endpoints.

Multiplying (7) and (9), we find
\[
\begin{aligned}
(G_{2(n-k)}H_{2k})(x,0,0)
&=(2n)_{\underline{2(n-k)}}(2k)!(-1)^k\binom nk
  (1+x)^{2k+2(n-k)}\\
&=(2n)!(-1)^k\binom nk(1+x)^{2n}. \tag{10}
\end{aligned}
\]
For the last equality we used
\[
(2n)_{\underline{2(n-k)}}(2k)!=(2n)!,
\]
because removing \(2(n-k)\) descending factors from \((2n)!\) leaves \((2k)!\).

Since
\[
[x^n](1+x)^{2n}=\binom{2n}{n},
\]
equation (10) gives
\[
[x^ny^0z^0](G_{2(n-k)}H_{2k})
=(2n)!(-1)^k\binom nk\binom{2n}{n}. \tag{11}
\]
Substitute (11) into (6). The sign \((-1)^k\) in (6) cancels the sign in (11), and hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
[x^ny^0z^0]D^nF_n
&=(2n)!\binom{2n}{n}
  \sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk^2. \tag{12}
\end{aligned}
\]

We use the standard Vandermonde identity
\[
\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk^2=\binom{2n}{n}. \tag{13}
\]
One direct proof is to compare coefficients of \(t^n\) in
\[
(1+t)^n(1+t)^n=(1+t)^{2n}.
\]
On the left, the coefficient is
\[
\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk\binom n{n-k}
=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk^2,
\]
using \(\binom n{n-k}=\binom nk\); on the right it is \(\binom{2n}{n}\). This proves (13). Therefore (12) becomes
\[
[x^ny^0z^0]D^nF_n
=(2n)!\binom{2n}{n}^2. \tag{14}
\]

Because \(\partial_y\) and \(\partial_z\) commute,
\[
D^n=(\partial_y\partial_z)^n=\partial_y^n\partial_z^n.
\]
Applying the coefficient relation (1) to \(P=F_n\), equation (14) therefore says
\[
(n!)^2[x^ny^nz^n]F_n
=(2n)!\binom{2n}{n}^2. \tag{15}
\]
Finally,
\[
(2n)!=\binom{2n}{n}(n!)^2.
\]
Substituting this into (15) gives
\[
(n!)^2[x^ny^nz^n]F_n
=(n!)^2\binom{2n}{n}^3.
\]
Since \(n!\ne0\), we may cancel \((n!)^2\), obtaining
\[
[x^ny^nz^n]F_n=\binom{2n}{n}^3.
\]
This argument also covers \(n=0\): all derivative orders are zero, both sides are \(1\), and the same factorial and binomial identities remain valid. Hence the identity holds for every \(n\ge0\), as claimed.
